## Course description

Project management as it is actually practiced: the quantitative core (work breakdown, critical
path method, PERT, earned value management) alongside adaptive delivery (Scrum, Kanban, flow
metrics), with hybrid approaches treated as the default real-world case rather than a compromise.
The course argues from empirical evidence rather than from convention — students learn to
distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic and to say what a project-success number is
actually measuring.

Running through every week is an AI layer. Students progress from grounded prompting, through
model-generated artifacts verified by code they write themselves, to specifying and building
agents that maintain live project artifacts — and to governing those agents, which is the
project-management problem the textbooks have not caught up with yet.

## Course objectives

By the end of the course a student can:

1. Decide which delivery approach fits a given project and defend the choice against a specific alternative.
2. Build and interpret the core quantitative artifacts: WBS, CPM network, PERT distribution, crash analysis, EVM report.
3. Run the adaptive artifacts: product backlog, sprint mechanics, cumulative flow diagram, Little's Law.
4. Read the evidence critically — distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic.
5. Diagnose a failing project and propose interventions ranked by expected effect, not by convention.
6. Specify, build, and govern an AI agent that maintains a live project artifact, and state what it got wrong.

### Additional expectations for students enrolled in IMSE 656

Students enrolled under the graduate number complete the same components at a
higher level of expectation:

- **Conceptual assignments** include an additional short-answer section requiring
  students to ground a claim in one of the primary sources on the [source shelf](ai.qmd#the-source-shelf).
- **Final project** must include a *methods justification* section: the choice of
  delivery approach, estimating method, and control mechanism defended against the
  empirical literature, with citations.
- **Final presentation** includes a five-minute defence against a challenge from the
  instructor drawn from the counter-evidence for the position taken.

## Required student resources

- **Optional textbook:** Larson &amp; Gray, *Project Management: The Managerial Process*,
  2024 Release, McGraw Hill. Chapter readings are listed weekly. Everything assessed
  is contained in the lecture notes on this site.
- **Course site:** <https://harunpirim.github.io/IMSE456> — notes, slides, recordings, labs.
- **Software:** a current LLM assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — free tiers are
  sufficient), a spreadsheet application, and Python via
  [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com) (no local install required).
  Scheduling exercises use [ProjectLibre](https://www.projectlibre.com/) or
  [Taiga](https://www.taiga.io/), both free.
- **Calculator** for the midterm. Programmable calculators and phones are not permitted.

## Evaluation procedures and criteria

| Component | Weight | What it is |
|:--|--:|:--|
| Conceptual assignments (MCQ) | 25% | Eight online multiple-choice sets, one per content block, on terms, theory, and the reasoning behind the methods. Auto-graded, lowest score dropped. |
| Studio assignments | 25% | Ten team deliverables produced in and after the Thursday studio sessions: WBS, CPM analysis, crash sequence, estimate comparison, EVM dashboard, risk register, flow simulation, approach defence, stakeholder map, case diagnosis. |
| Midterm examination | 20% | **Thursday 15 October, in class.** Closed notes, closed book, no computers or phones. Covers Weeks 1–7. |
| Final project | 30% | A semester-long project conducted with an industry partner. Four milestones plus a final report and presentation. See [Final Project](project.qmd). |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,10,56]"}

| Grade | Percentage of total |
|:--|:--|
| A | ≥ 90.00% |
| B | 80.00 – 89.99% |
| C | 70.00 – 79.99% |
| D | 60.00 – 69.99% |
| F | < 60.00% |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

### Late work

Conceptual assignments close at the posted time and do not reopen; the lowest score is
dropped to absorb one missed set. Studio assignments lose 10% per calendar day, to a floor
of 50%, for five days, after which they are not accepted. Final project milestones are
firm because a partner organization is waiting on them — contact the instructor **before**
the deadline if a milestone is at risk.

### Feedback turnaround

Conceptual assignments are graded automatically and available immediately. Studio
assignments are returned within seven days. Project milestones are returned within
fourteen days.

## Attendance

According to [NDSU Policy 333](https://www.ndsu.edu/fileadmin/policy/333.pdf), attendance
in classes is expected. Students should contact the instructor as soon as possible to notify
them of any extended illness or family emergency that might warrant an extension on assignments.

Attendance is not directly a component of the course grade. However, studio assignments are
produced in teams during Thursday sessions, and a student who is absent contributes nothing
to that deliverable — attendance is therefore consequential in practice even though it is
not scored.

Veterans and student service members with special circumstances or who are activated are
encouraged to notify the instructor as soon as possible and are encouraged to provide
Activation Orders.

## Artificial intelligence policy

AI use is **expected**, not merely permitted. Much of this course is about using these tools
well. Three rules make that workable:

1. **Label it.** Any submitted artifact that an AI system produced or substantially drafted
   says so, names the tool, and includes the prompt or a link to the conversation.
2. **Verify it.** Every quantitative result generated by a model must be accompanied by the
   code or hand calculation that checks it. A number you cannot verify is a number you did
   not produce. This is graded.
3. **Own it.** You are responsible for everything you submit, including the parts a model
   wrote. "The AI said so" is not a defence, in this course or in a project review.

The **midterm is the exception**: it is closed-book, closed-notes, and computer-free,
because the reasoning it tests is the reasoning you need when the tool is unavailable or wrong.

## Code of ethics

Students are expected to be familiar with the

Projects conducted with industry partners raise real questions of confidentiality,

## What this course deliberately does not cover

Stating exclusions explicitly is more useful than pretending to comprehensiveness:

- **PMP exam drilling.** The exam changes; the reasoning does not. The credential is
  mentioned, not taught to.
- **Tool tutorials** (MS Project, Jira, Primavera). One is assigned as homework
  infrastructure; no lecture time goes to menus.
- **The full process catalogue of PMBOK 8.** You learn the *shape* of a process standard
  and how to look things up. Memorizing inputs-tools-outputs is the lowest-value activity
  in project-management education.
- **Scaling frameworks in depth** (SAFe, LeSS, Nexus). One segment on why they exist and
  why the evidence for them is thin.
- **Six Sigma and lean manufacturing.** Adjacent field, separate course.
- **Contract law.** Contract *types* and incentive structure are covered; the law is not.
